Delhi Sultanate – art, architecture, language and literature
Mughal Empire – socio-economic and religious conditions
Mughal Empire – art, architecture, language and literature
Shivaji and the rise of Maratha Empire

official_questions.stem: In the Third Battle of Panipat, the Marathas were defeated by the
official_questions.core_fact: In the Third Battle of Panipat (14 Jan 1761) Ahmad Shah Abdali (Afghan) defeated the Marathas under Sadashivrao Bhau; Rohillas (Najib-ud-Daula) and Awadh allied with Abdali.

statements.t: In the Third Battle of Panipat, the Marathas were defeated by the English.
In the Third Battle of Panipat, the Marathas were defeated by the Ruhelas.
statements.m: true fact not the one asked
statements.fact: Rohillas were allies; the victor was the Afghan Abdali.

statements.t: In the Third Battle of Panipat, the Marathas were defeated by the Afghans.
In the Third Battle of Panipat, the Marathas were defeated by the Mughals.

official_questions.rule: Panipat I 1526 (Babur-Ibrahim Lodi), II 1556 (Akbar-Hemu), III 1761 (Abdali-Marathas).

official_questions.stem: Ramanuja preached
official_questions.core_fact: Ramanuja (11th-12th c.) propounded Vishishtadvaita and emphasised bhakti (prapatti) as the path to salvation.

statements.t: Ramanuja preached ahimsa.
Ramanuja preached bhakti.
Ramanuja preached gyan.
statements.fact: Jnana is Shankara's path; Ramanuja's is bhakti.

statements.t: Ramanuja preached the Vedas.
statements.fact: Dayananda preached return to the Vedas.

official_questions.rule: Shankara - Advaita/jnana; Ramanuja - Vishishtadvaita/bhakti; Madhva - Dvaita.

official_questions.stem: Fort St. George was built by the English at
official_questions.core_fact: Fort St. George was built by the English (Francis Day, Andrew Cogan) at Madrasapatnam in 1639-44 on land from Damarla Venkatadri Nayaka.

statements.t: Fort St. George was built by the English at Madrasapatnam.
Fort St. George was built by the English at Nagapatnam.
Fort St. George was built by the English at Duggarajapatnam.
Fort St. George was built by the English at Machilipatnam.
statements.m: true fact not the one asked
statements.fact: Machilipatnam had the first factory; Fort St. George is at Madras.

official_questions.rule: English: Masulipatnam 1611 -> Armagaon 1626 -> Madras (Fort St. George) 1639-40.

official_questions.stem: Who was known as "Lakh Baksh" ?
official_questions.core_fact: Qutb-ud-din Aibak was called Lakh Baksh ('giver of lakhs') for his generosity.

statements.t: Aibak was known as 'Lakh Baksh'.
Iltutmish was known as 'Lakh Baksh'.
Razia was known as 'Lakh Baksh'.
Balban was known as 'Lakh Baksh'.

official_questions.rule: Aibak - Lakh Baksh; Balban - Zil-i-Ilahi, blood and iron.

official_questions.stem: The "Kadagam" under the Cholas was
official_questions.core_fact: Under the Cholas, 'kadagam' meant a military cantonment/camp.

statements.t: The 'Kadagam' under the Cholas was Revenue department.
The 'Kadagam' under the Cholas was Port town.
The 'Kadagam' under the Cholas was Army cantonment.
The 'Kadagam' under the Cholas was Market-place.

official_questions.rule: Chola: mandalam > valanadu > nadu > kurram; ur, sabha, nagaram assemblies; kadagam = cantonment.

official_questions.stem: The Sufi order which adopted regular yogic practices was
official_questions.core_fact: The Chishti order in India absorbed local practices including yogic breathing (habs-i-dam), sama (music); APPSC's corrected key is Chishti.

statements.t: The Sufi order which adopted regular yogic practices was the Qadri.
The Sufi order which adopted regular yogic practices was the Suhrawardi.
statements.fact: Suhrawardis were orthodox; Chishtis adopted yogic practices.

statements.t: The Sufi order which adopted regular yogic practices was the Chishti.
The Sufi order which adopted regular yogic practices was the Naqshbandi.

official_questions.rule: Chishti (Muinuddin, Ajmer) - sama, yoga influence; Naqshbandi orthodox; Suhrawardi accepted state grants.
official_questions.key_note: Corrected final key; some sources associate the Naqshbandis/Shattaris with yogic breathing.

official_questions.stem: Who founded the 'Khalsa' in Sikhism ?
official_questions.core_fact: Guru Gobind Singh founded the Khalsa at Anandpur Sahib on Baisakhi 1699.

statements.t: The 'Khalsa' in Sikhism was founded by Guru Govind Singh.
The 'Khalsa' in Sikhism was founded by Guru Tegh Bahadur.
statements.fact: Tegh Bahadur was executed by Aurangzeb.

statements.t: The 'Khalsa' in Sikhism was founded by Guru Arjan Dev.
statements.m: true fact not the one asked
statements.fact: Arjan Dev compiled the Adi Granth.

statements.t: The 'Khalsa' in Sikhism was founded by Guru Ramdas.
statements.m: true fact not the one asked

official_questions.rule: Ramdas - Amritsar; Arjan - Adi Granth; Tegh Bahadur - martyrdom; Gobind Singh - Khalsa 1699.

official_questions.stem: The Mughal emperor who did not patronise historians and musicians was
official_questions.core_fact: Aurangzeb discontinued official history writing (after 10 years) and banned court music; Babur, Jahangir and Shah Jahan patronised historians/musicians.

statements.t: The Mughal emperor who did not patronise historians and musicians was Babar.
statements.m: true fact not the one asked

statements.t: The Mughal emperor who did not patronise historians and musicians was Jahangir.
statements.m: true fact not the one asked

statements.t: The Mughal emperor who did not patronise historians and musicians was Shah Jahan.
statements.m: true fact not the one asked

statements.t: The Mughal emperor who did not patronise historians and musicians was Aurangzeb.

official_questions.rule: Aurangzeb banned music & history-writing, yet the best works on music (Persian) were written in his reign.
official_questions.key_note: Historians note Aurangzeb himself played the veena and many Persian music works date from his reign; key retained.

official_questions.stem: The Sultan who first abolished the system of farming taxes was
official_questions.core_fact: Firoz Shah Tughlaq revived revenue farming (ijara); Alauddin Khalji curbed intermediaries; Ghiyasuddin Tughlaq's and Muhammad Tughlaq's revenue policies are variously described - no clean 'first abolished' fact.

statements.t: Mubarak Khilji was the Sultan who first abolished the system of farming taxes.
Ghiasuddin Tughlak was the Sultan who first abolished the system of farming taxes.
Mohammad-Bin-Tughlak was the Sultan who first abolished the system of farming taxes.
Feroz Tughlak was the Sultan who first abolished the system of farming taxes.
statements.fact: Firoz Tughlaq revived (did not abolish) revenue farming.

official_questions.rule: Firoz Tughlaq: hereditary iqtas, revenue farming revived, jaziya on Brahmins.
official_questions.key_note: Deleted (cancelled) by APPSC in the final key.

official_questions.stem: Why did Alauddin Khilji introduce a market policy of fixed prices for food grains ?
options: For better return to the farmers
To ensure that consumers can directly purchase from farmers
To ensure that the market price is equal to the fair price
To ensure that soldiers can live comfortably with low salary
official_questions.key: To ensure that soldiers can live comfortably with low salary
official_questions.core_fact: Alauddin Khalji fixed low prices of grain and other goods so that a large standing army (raised against Mongol threats) could be maintained on low salaries.

statements.t: Alauddin Khalji introduced fixed grain prices for better return to the farmers.
statements.d: For better return to the farmers
statements.fact: Prices were fixed low; peasants had to sell cheap – the measure did not favour farmers.

statements.t: Alauddin Khalji introduced fixed grain prices to ensure that consumers can directly purchase from farmers.
statements.d: To ensure that consumers can directly purchase from farmers
statements.fact: Grain was brought through registered merchants (karwanis) to state-controlled markets.

statements.t: Alauddin Khalji introduced fixed grain prices to ensure that the market price is equal to the fair price.
statements.m: true fact not the one asked
statements.d: To ensure that the market price is equal to the fair price
statements.fact: Fixed prices were the means; the aim was cheap supplies for a low-paid army.

statements.t: Alauddin Khalji introduced fixed grain prices to ensure that soldiers can live comfortably with low salary.
statements.d: To ensure that soldiers can live comfortably with low salary

official_questions.rule: Alauddin's market reforms: purpose = army on low pay; agencies = shahna-i-mandi, diwan-i-riyasat; source = Barani.

official_questions.stem: Which of these Sultans set up a Department of Public Works to look after building programmes ?
official_questions.core_fact: Firoz Shah Tughlaq (1351-88) created a Department of Public Works to build canals, towns (Firozabad, Hisar, Jaunpur), mosques and repair monuments.

statements.t: Firoz Tughlaq set up a Department of Public Works to look after building programmes.
Jalaluddin Tughlaq set up a Department of Public Works to look after building programmes.
statements.fact: Jalaluddin was a Khalji, not a Tughlaq; the PWD was Firoz's.

statements.t: Muhammad Bin Tughlaq set up a Department of Public Works to look after building programmes.
statements.fact: Muhammad bin Tughlaq is known for token currency and Diwan-i-Kohi; the PWD was Firoz's.

statements.t: Ghiyasuddin Tughlaq set up a Department of Public Works to look after building programmes.
statements.fact: Ghiyasuddin built Tughlaqabad but the PWD was set up by Firoz.

official_questions.rule: Firoz: Diwan-i-Khairat, Diwan-i-Bandagan, PWD, canals (Yamuna), jizya on Brahmins; MbT: Diwan-i-Kohi, token currency.

official_questions.stem: The Silver Rupiya, which remained a standard currency for centuries was introduced by
official_questions.core_fact: Sher Shah Suri (1540-45) introduced the silver rupiya (about 178 grains), which remained standard under the Mughals and the British.

statements.t: The silver rupiya, a standard currency for centuries, was introduced by Akbar.
statements.fact: Akbar continued Sher Shah's rupiya; he did not introduce it.

statements.t: The silver rupiya, a standard currency for centuries, was introduced by Sher Shah Suri.
The silver rupiya, a standard currency for centuries, was introduced by Jahangir.
statements.fact: Jahangir issued zodiac coins; the rupiya was Sher Shah's.

statements.t: The silver rupiya, a standard currency for centuries, was introduced by Humayun.
statements.fact: Humayun was defeated by Sher Shah, who introduced the rupiya.

official_questions.rule: Sher Shah: rupiya (silver), dam (copper), Grand Trunk Road, sarais, patta-qabuliyat.

official_questions.stem: The "Dahsala" system developed by Raja Todar Mal was for
options: Collection of revenue at standard rate which was valid for 10 years
Measurement of land once in 10 years for fixing area of assessment
Collection of revenue on the basis of average of produce and prices in the last 10 years
Sharing of crop between the farmer and the State for 10 years
official_questions.key: Collection of revenue on the basis of average of produce and prices in the last 10 years
official_questions.core_fact: Under Akbar's Dahsala (1580), the average produce and the average prices of the previous ten years (1570-80) were used to fix a cash revenue demand per crop per bigha.

statements.t: The Dahsala system was for collection of revenue at a standard rate valid for 10 years.
statements.d: Collection of revenue at standard rate which was valid for 10 years
statements.fact: Dahsala did not fix a rate valid for 10 years; it used the 10-year average of produce and prices.

statements.t: The Dahsala system was for measurement of land once in 10 years for fixing the area of assessment.
statements.d: Measurement of land once in 10 years for fixing area of assessment
statements.fact: Land was measured (zabt) but Dahsala's 10 years refers to averaging, not measurement intervals.

statements.t: The Dahsala system was for collection of revenue on the basis of the average of produce and prices in the last 10 years.
statements.d: Collection of revenue on the basis of average of produce and prices in the last 10 years

statements.t: The Dahsala system was for sharing of crop between the farmer and the State for 10 years.
statements.d: Sharing of crop between the farmer and the State for 10 years
statements.fact: Crop-sharing (batai) was a different method; Dahsala fixed cash rates.

official_questions.rule: Dahsala/Zabti: 10-year average of produce & prices -> cash rates (dasturs); not a 10-year settlement (that misreading is the standard trap).

official_questions.stem: The class of traders who specialized in carrying bulk goods over long distances during Mughal period were called
official_questions.core_fact: Banjaras were itinerant trader-carriers who moved bulk goods (grain, salt) over long distances on pack-oxen caravans.

statements.t: During the Mughal period the traders who specialised in carrying bulk goods over long distances were called Beoparis.
statements.fact: Beoparis/vyaparis were merchants; the long-distance bulk carriers were Banjaras.

statements.t: During the Mughal period the traders who specialised in carrying bulk goods over long distances were called Baniks.
During the Mughal period the traders who specialised in carrying bulk goods over long distances were called Sarafs.
statements.fact: Sarrafs dealt in money-changing, hundis and banking.

statements.t: During the Mughal period the traders who specialised in carrying bulk goods over long distances were called Banjaras.

official_questions.rule: Banjaras = bulk carriers; Sarrafs = bankers/hundi; Banias = traders; Mahajans = moneylenders.

official_questions.stem: During Mughal period, approximately how much percentage of rural agricultural produce was marketed ?
official_questions.core_fact: Per APPSC's key, about 20% of rural agricultural produce was marketed in the Mughal period (historians' estimates vary).

statements.t: During the Mughal period approximately 10% of rural agricultural produce was marketed.
During the Mughal period approximately 15% of rural agricultural produce was marketed.
During the Mughal period approximately 20% of rural agricultural produce was marketed.
During the Mughal period approximately 25% of rural agricultural produce was marketed.

official_questions.rule: Treat Mughal 'marketed share' as a disputed estimate; remember APPSC's figure for this paper.
official_questions.key_note: App notes (1:135:3) record 15% as APPSC's printed key in PYQ copies and an older 25%; this job's key (revised) is 20% (option 3). Key kept; the figure is an estimate without a standard source.

official_questions.stem: Who said the following about 18th century India, "Bear in mind that the commerce of India is the commerce of the world" ?
official_questions.core_fact: Peter the Great of Russia is credited with: 'Bear in mind that the commerce of India is the commerce of the world, and he who can exclusively command it is the dictator of Europe.'

statements.t: Peter the Great, of Russia said 'Bear in mind that the commerce of India is the commerce of the world'.
Vasco da Gama said 'Bear in mind that the commerce of India is the commerce of the world'.
statements.fact: Vasco da Gama opened the sea route; the quote is attributed to Peter the Great.

statements.t: Robert Clive said 'Bear in mind that the commerce of India is the commerce of the world'.
Dupleix, the French Governor General said 'Bear in mind that the commerce of India is the commerce of the world'.

official_questions.rule: Peter the Great's quote is used to show India's pull on European powers; not a European trader in India.

official_questions.stem: Which one of the following pairs is not correctly matched ?
official_questions.core_fact: Khanwa 1527 (Babur vs Rana Sanga); Haldighati 1576 (Akbar's army vs Maharana Pratap); Bilgram/Kannauj 1540 (Humayun lost to Sher Shah); Chausa 1539 (Humayun lost to Sher Shah) – not Jahangir.

statements.t: Babur – Battle of Khanwa is not correctly matched.
Akbar – Battle of Haldighati is not correctly matched.
Humayun – Battle of Bilgram is not correctly matched.
Jahangir – Battle of Chausa is not correctly matched.

official_questions.rule: Humayun's two defeats by Sher Shah: Chausa 1539, Kannauj/Bilgram 1540; Jahangir fought no such battle.

official_questions.stem: Who among the following introduced the Blue Water Policy ?
official_questions.core_fact: Francisco de Almeida (first Portuguese Viceroy, 1505-09) followed the Blue Water Policy – Portuguese supremacy at sea rather than land conquest.

statements.t: Alfonso de Albuquerque introduced the Blue Water Policy.
statements.fact: Albuquerque took Goa and built forts; Almeida introduced the Blue Water Policy.

statements.t: Pedro Alvares Cabral introduced the Blue Water Policy.
Francisco de Almeida introduced the Blue Water Policy.
Nino da Cunha introduced the Blue Water Policy.
statements.fact: Nino da Cunha shifted the HQ to Goa.

official_questions.rule: Almeida – Blue Water (1505-09); Albuquerque – Goa 1510, real founder; Nino da Cunha – Goa capital 1530.

official_questions.stem:
Consider the following statements :
a. Humayun brought famous painters Mir Sayyid Ali and Abdus Samad from Iran to Delhi.
b. Jahangir's reign is considered as the 'Golden period of the Mughal painting'.
c. During the reign of Jahangir, European painting was introduced at the Mughal court by the Danish merchants.
Which of the statements given above is/are incorrect ?
official_questions.core_fact: Humayun brought Mir Sayyid Ali and Abdus Samad from Safavid Iran; Jahangir's reign was the golden age of Mughal painting; European art reached the court through Portuguese Jesuits under Akbar (and English envoys under Jahangir), not Danish merchants.

statements.t: Humayun brought the painters Mir Sayyid Ali and Abdus Samad from Iran to Delhi.
statements.d: Mir Sayyid Ali and Abdus Samad

statements.t: Jahangir's reign is considered the 'Golden period of Mughal painting'.
During Jahangir's reign European painting was introduced at the Mughal court by Danish merchants.
statements.fact: European painting came via Portuguese Jesuit missions under Akbar; under Jahangir, the English (Thomas Roe) presented paintings.

official_questions.rule: Mughal painting: Humayun – Persian masters; Akbar – atelier, Jesuit/European influence; Jahangir – golden age; Shah Jahan – decline begins.

official_questions.stem:
Match List I with List II and select the correct answer using the codes given below the lists :
List I (Delhi Sultans) - List II (Reforms)
a. Muhammad bin Tughlaq - I. Branding of Horses
b. Alauddin Khalji - II. Token Currency
c. Iltutmish - III. Development of Irrigation
d. Firuz Shah Tughlaq - IV. Introducing Silver Tankas
official_questions.core_fact: Muhammad bin Tughlaq – token currency (1329-30); Alauddin Khalji – branding of horses (dagh) and descriptive rolls (huliya); Iltutmish – silver tanka and copper jital; Firoz Shah Tughlaq – irrigation canals.

statements.t: Muhammad bin Tughlaq introduced token currency.
Alauddin Khalji introduced branding of horses.
Iltutmish introduced silver tankas.
Firoz Shah Tughlaq developed irrigation.
Muhammad bin Tughlaq introduced branding of horses.
Firoz Shah Tughlaq introduced silver tankas.
statements.fact: Silver tanka was introduced by Iltutmish.

statements.t: Iltutmish introduced token currency.
statements.fact: Token currency was Muhammad bin Tughlaq's.

official_questions.rule: Sultanate signatures: Iltutmish tanka/iqta; Balban sijda/paibos; Alauddin dagh/market; MbT token/Diwan-i-Kohi; Firoz canals/PWD.

official_questions.stem: Among Ashtapradhans of Shivaji, the Sar-i-Naubat was associated with which of the following tasks ?
official_questions.core_fact: In Shivaji's Ashtapradhan, the Sar-i-Naubat (Senapati) was the commander-in-chief of the army.

statements.t: Among Shivaji's Ashtapradhans, the Sar-i-Naubat was the Finance Minister.
Among Shivaji's Ashtapradhans, the Sar-i-Naubat was the Military Commander.
Among Shivaji's Ashtapradhans, the Sar-i-Naubat was the Foreign Secretary.
Among Shivaji's Ashtapradhans, the Sar-i-Naubat was the Revenue Minister.

official_questions.rule: Ashtapradhan: Peshwa (PM), Amatya (finance), Mantri/Waqia-navis, Sachiv/Surunavis (correspondence), Sumant/Dabir (foreign), Senapati/Sar-i-Naubat (army), Panditrao (religion), Nyayadhish (justice).
